name: Buccal fat removal
lead: Buccal fat removal, also called bichectomy or buccal fat pad extraction, is a cosmetic operation that takes out part of the buccal fat pad (Bichat's fat pad), a deep encapsulated pad of fat in each cheek, to slim the lower midface and create a more contoured or hollow-cheeked look. It is usually done through a small incision inside the mouth.[1][3][9]

Looksmaxxing communities discuss it as a hardmaxxing option for people who stay round-faced even when lean. Surgical reviews describe it as generally safe with careful anatomical technique, but the evidence is mainly case series and small single-arm studies, and the fat pad does not regrow after removal.[2][3][9]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies and 308 patients reported an overall postoperative complication prevalence of 25%, mostly swelling, trismus and pain, with high heterogeneity between studies; serious events such as facial nerve paralysis, infection and hematoma were rare in that analysis.[4] Wikipedia notes that removal carries a risk of damage to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and to the parotid duct.[8][9]

paras: The buccal fat pad is an encapsulated mass of fat lying between the buccinator muscle and superficial muscles such as the masseter and zygomaticus, and is distinct from the more superficial malar fat pad. It is described as having several lobes and extensions, and its anterior part surrounds the parotid duct. Proposed functions include aiding movement of the chewing muscles and cushioning facial muscles.[8]

A review explains that although the pad has similar histology to fat elsewhere, its fibrous capsule means it is not metabolised in the way other fat depots are, which is why proponents say it stays full in lean people.[1]

Reviews describe an intraoral approach using blunt dissection and suction-assisted extraction of the pad. The aim is to reduce volume in the lower third of the face and sharpen contours.[1][3] Wikipedia describes the operation as taking about 30 minutes under local anesthesia, with swelling lasting days and final results taking up to about three months, and notes that it is sometimes combined with facelifts, chin implants or neck lifts.[9]
An 'extended' variant that also removes the buccal extension and part of the temporal extension has been described for more extreme cheek contouring.[7]

A single-arm trial of 21 patients measured pain, swelling, trismus, facial volume, satisfaction and oral-health-related quality of life up to three months after partial removal.[6] A case series of 643 procedures by two surgeons reported a low incidence of major complications, which fell further with use of a compressive bandage.[2]

Authors of the extended-bichectomy paper state that long-term results of conventional approaches are generally accepted to have limitations and that the operation does not always deliver satisfactory results.[7] Wikipedia notes that the effect is permanent, that long-term research is limited, and that removal may produce a gaunt appearance as cheeks lose volume with age.[9]

The 2025 meta-analysis listed edema (38.4% of the complications), trismus (30.1%), pain (19.4%), asymmetry (11.7%), and rarer facial nerve paralysis, infection, hematoma and emphysema; all occurred postoperatively.[4] A literature review of bichectomy complications states that the operation is linked to potentially serious complications because of the local anatomy, with some sequelae temporary and some permanent.[1]

Parotid duct injury and sialocele are reported as uncommon but significant, and case reports and a small series describe salivary duct injury after facial cosmetic procedures including buccal fat removal.[5]

The pad was first described by Lorenz Heister in 1732 as a gland and identified as fat by Xavier Bichat in 1802. Interest in cosmetic removal rose in the early 2020s after a public figure disclosed having it done in 2021, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons began tracking it in 2022. The procedure is also nicknamed 'Handsome Squidward surgery' online.[9]

Human data include a single-arm CONSORT-guided trial in 21 patients,[6] a 643-case retrospective series,[2] a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies,[4] and registered studies of intraoral and hydrodissection techniques.[10] No randomised trial comparing removal with no treatment or with alternatives was found.

Forum threads ask whether leaning out is sufficient, whether the operation suits a particular face, and how long swelling lasts, and there are threads recounting results, a 'confirmed botch' and a procedure that 'went wrong'.[11][12][13][14] Members also discuss whether removal is advisable for a young person who still has rounder cheeks.[15]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the procedure is debated as a way to get hollow cheeks, with threads about candidacy, results and botched outcomes.[11][12][13][14][15]

claims.claim: Buccal fat removal gives leaner, more sculpted cheeks that dieting cannot.
claims.believers: Proponents say the buccal pad does not shrink with leanness, so some lean people keep full cheeks, and report results in threads asking whether the operation is warranted.[11][15]
claims.experts: Reviews describe the pad as encapsulated and describe the intended lower-face volume reduction, and a 21-patient trial measured facial volume reduction after partial removal.[1][6]

claims.claim: Removal can leave a person looking gaunt or worse than before.
claims.believers: Threads such as 'gone wrong' and 'confirmed botch' reflect members warning that results can look worse, especially with ageing.[12][13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes removal may leave a gaunt look as cheeks naturally lose volume with age, and surgeons describe an extended removal as sometimes limited or unsatisfactory in results.[7][9]

claims.claim: The operation is low-risk and minor.
claims.believers: Members post recovery photos and multi-month updates of the operation in threads on the topic.[14]
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis found 25% prevalence of postoperative complications, mostly mild; rarer events include facial nerve paralysis, and parotid duct injury is reported.[4][5]

claims.claim: Fat grafting can restore volume if removal goes too far.
claims.believers: Community write-ups state that the pad will not return to normal but fat transfer can partly compensate.[15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists fat injections, dermal fat grafts and fillers as alternatives and states the fat does not regrow; no trials of grafting after bichectomy were found.[9]

card.summary: Intraoral removal of the cheek's buccal fat pad for a slimmer, hollower look; permanent, with a 25% pooled postoperative complication rate and no randomised trials.
card.note: Irreversible; facial nerve and parotid duct injury are reported, and a gaunt look with ageing is discussed.

quick.overview:
Buccal fat removal takes out part of the deep fat pad in each cheek through a small cut inside the mouth, aiming for a slimmer lower face and more visible cheekbone contour. It became widely discussed on social media in the early 2020s and is a common hardmaxxing topic on looksmaxxing forums.

Published evidence is mostly case series, a small single-arm trial and systematic reviews. Surgeons describe it as generally safe with careful anatomy, while forum users share both satisfied and botched outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The encapsulated pad is extracted by blunt dissection and suction through an intraoral incision, permanently reducing cheek volume. Because the pad is not lost with general weight loss, proponents say removal changes contour where dieting does not.
quick.risks: A 2025 meta-analysis of 308 patients reported 25% prevalence of postoperative complications, mainly swelling, trismus, pain and asymmetry, with rare facial nerve paralysis, infection or hematoma. Parotid duct injury is reported. The effect is permanent and may look gaunt with ageing, according to encyclopedia summaries.
